solution.concept_anchor: First Peshwa under Shivaji's Ashtapradhan
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Balaji Vishwanath is widely associated with the consolidation of Peshwa power and is often loosely called the 'first Peshwa', causing students to overlook the original ministerial appointment under Shivaji.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Balaji Vishwanath — he was the first powerful hereditary Peshwa but not the first person to hold the office under Shivaji.
Eliminate Baji Rao I — he succeeded Balaji Vishwanath and is known for military conquests, not the original appointment.
Eliminate Ramchandra Pant Amatya — he was a regency figure, not the first Peshwa under Shivaji's Ashtapradhan.
Confirm Moropant Trimbak Pingle — appointed as the first Peshwa under Shivaji's eight-minister council.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A student who has read broadly about the Peshwa era will associate the Peshwa's rise to prominence with Balaji Vishwanath and pick option (a). The trap exploits the conflation of 'first Peshwa as a powerful office' with 'first holder of the Peshwa title'. Balaji Vishwanath transformed the Peshwaship into a hereditary dominant office, but Moropant Trimbak Pingle was the original appointee under Shivaji's Ashtapradhan. This is a classic entity-swap trap where the more famous name displaces the historically accurate first holder.
solution.final_explanation:
Under Chhatrapati Shivaji's administrative system, the Ashtapradhan (council of eight ministers) included the Peshwa as the chief minister responsible for general administration. This was originally a ministerial appointment, not a hereditary office.

• Option (a) — Balaji Vishwanath: Incorrect. He was the first Peshwa to make the office hereditary and dominant, but he was not the original appointee under Shivaji.
• Option (b) — Moropant Trimbak Pingle: Correct. He was appointed the first Peshwa under Shivaji's Ashtapradhan system, holding the office in its original ministerial capacity.
• Option (c) — Ramchandra Pant Amatya: Incorrect. He served as regent during a later period of Maratha history; he was Amatya (finance minister), not the first Peshwa.
• Option (d) — Baji Rao I: Incorrect. He was the most celebrated Peshwa for military campaigns but served in the early 18th century, long after Shivaji.

Value Addition:
• The Peshwa was originally the first among equals in the Ashtapradhan.
• Balaji Vishwanath (1713–1720) converted the office into a hereditary prime ministership.
• After Shivaji, the Ashtapradhan gradually lost collective authority as individual offices gained dominance.

solution.concept_anchor: 1719 Treaty terms — Maratha-Mughal revenue rights

statement_analysis.statement: The 1719 agreement secured Chauth and Sardeshmukhi collection rights for the Marathas over the Deccan provinces.
statement_analysis.reason: The treaty brokered through the Sayyid Brothers explicitly granted Marathas Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights over Deccan — the first formal Mughal recognition of these revenue claims.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of 1719 resulted in the cession of the territory of Malwa to the Marathas.
statement_analysis.reason: Malwa was ceded to the Marathas under the Treaty of Bhopal in 1738, not in 1719; the 1719 agreement gave revenue rights, not territorial sovereignty.

statement_analysis.statement: Hussain Ali and Abdullah Khan, the Sayyid Brothers, acted as intermediaries who enabled Maratha recognition by the Mughal court.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sayyid Brothers were the dominant kingmakers at the Mughal court during this period of imperial instability and brokered the deal that released Shahu and recognized Maratha revenue rights.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who recall 'Malwa' as a major Maratha acquisition will conflate the 1738 territorial cession with the 1719 revenue-rights agreement, making statements 1 and 3 seem wrong.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — the 1719 treaty is specifically associated with Chauth and Sardeshmukhi recognition over the Deccan; this is a key fact.
Eliminate Statement 2 — Malwa's cession belongs to 1738 (Treaty of Bhopal), not 1719; any option including Statement 2 as correct is wrong.
Confirm Statement 3 — the Sayyid Brothers' kingmaker role at the Mughal court is well-documented in this context.
Only option (a) — Statements 1 and 3 — satisfies both confirmed facts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the tendency to merge two major Mughal-Maratha agreements: the 1719 treaty (revenue rights) and the 1738 Treaty of Bhopal (territorial cession of Malwa). A student who remembers that Malwa came to the Marathas through a Mughal agreement but forgets the exact year will accept Statement 2 as correct and be pulled toward option (b) or (d). The 1719 agreement was a watershed in Maratha legitimacy — but it granted fiscal rights, not territorial sovereignty.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1719 treaty brokered by the Sayyid Brothers represented the first formal Mughal acknowledgment of Maratha claims. It secured the release of Chhatrapati Shahu and recognized Maratha rights to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from the Deccan.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Revenue collection rights (Chauth and Sardeshmukhi) over Deccan were explicitly granted. This was qualitatively significant as the Mughal empire legitimized Maratha fiscal authority.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The cession of Malwa as a territory came only under the Treaty of Bhopal (1738), signed after Baji Rao I's northern campaigns. The 1719 agreement conferred no territorial sovereignty.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Sayyid Brothers (Hussain Ali and Abdullah Khan) were the de facto controllers of the Mughal throne during the post-Aurangzeb chaos and were instrumental in this settlement.

Value Addition:
• The 1719 treaty is often called a watershed in Maratha legitimacy — it transformed Maratha claims from military extortion to treaty-recognized rights.
• Balaji Vishwanath personally travelled to Delhi to negotiate this agreement, demonstrating early Peshwa diplomatic skill.
• The Sayyid Brothers' power ended shortly after when they were overthrown by the Nizam faction.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Palkhed vs Battle of Bhopal — distinct outcomes

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Palkhed (1728) was fought between Baji Rao I and the Nizam-ul-Mulk, resulting in the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon.
statement_analysis.reason: Palkhed (1728) was indeed Baji Rao I's strategic masterpiece against Nizam-ul-Mulk; its outcome was the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon in which the Nizam acknowledged Maratha rights to Chauth and Sardeshmukhi.

statement_analysis.statement: Baji Rao I's primary tactical innovation at Palkhed was the use of superior artillery to overcome the Nizam's defensive formations.
statement_analysis.reason: Baji Rao's triumph at Palkhed was built on maneuver warfare — cutting off the Nizam's supply lines and forcing a surrender without pitched battle; artillery superiority was not the factor, and this description better fits later engagements.

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Bhopal (1738) and the Battle of Palkhed (1728) were both fought against the same opponent and produced identical treaty outcomes.
statement_analysis.reason: While both involved the Nizam as a party, the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon (1728) acknowledged revenue rights, whereas the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) addressed Mughal cession of Malwa — the opponents and outcomes were distinct.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is entirely correct, so students looking for the 'NOT correct' answer may over-focus on verifying it and accept one of the fabricated incorrect statements without scrutiny.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Palkhed (1728) vs. Nizam, Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon is a well-established fact; this statement is NOT the answer.
Identify Statement 2 as incorrect — Palkhed's fame rests on supply-line maneuver warfare, not artillery dominance; artillery advantage is associated with Ibrahim Khan Gardi at Panipat III.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — the two battles had different coalition compositions and different treaty terms; calling them identical is factually wrong.
Option (c) names Statements 2 and 3 as NOT correct — this matches the analysis.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the conflation between Palkhed (1728) and Bhopal (1738) — two Maratha-Nizam engagements that students habitually merge. Statement 3 is deliberately designed to sound plausible by noting both involved the Nizam, which is true. The trap is that the outcomes and treaty terms were qualitatively different. Statement 2 exploits the tendency to associate 'great battle victory' with artillery — a feature that actually characterised Panipat III, not Palkhed.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao I's 1728 campaign against Nizam-ul-Mulk is celebrated in military history for its maneuver-based strategy rather than direct confrontation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Palkhed (1728) against Nizam-ul-Mulk produced the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon. The Nizam was compelled to acknowledge Maratha revenue rights.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Palkhed victory was achieved through interdiction of supply lines, forcing the Nizam into a strategically untenable position — not through artillery superiority. Artillery as a decisive factor is associated with the Panipat III context.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Though both Palkhed and Bhopal involved the Nizam, their contexts and treaty outcomes differed. Mungi-Shegaon (1728) addressed Deccan revenue rights; the Bhopal settlement (1738) related to Malwa's cession from the Mughals.

Value Addition:
• Palkhed is considered one of the finest examples of cavalry-based strategic maneuver in Indian military history.
• The Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon established Maratha dominance in the Deccan as a structural reality.
• Baji Rao fought the Nizam at least twice — students must link each battle to its specific treaty.

Maratha Revenue System — Chauth, Sardeshmukhi, and Mokasa

solution.concept_anchor: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi — correct proportions and distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: Chauth: One-fourth of assessed land revenue collected by Marathas from non-Maratha territories as a protection levy
statement_analysis.reason: Chauth was precisely 1/4th (25%) of revenue — a protection tax that did not imply direct Maratha administration of the territory.

statement_analysis.statement: Sardeshmukhi: An additional levy of one-tenth of revenue claimed by the Peshwa as a hereditary right over the Deccan
statement_analysis.reason: Sardeshmukhi was 10% of revenue — claimed as a hereditary right by the Maratha chief (originally Shivaji) as the senior headman (Sardeshmukh) of the Deccan.

statement_analysis.statement: Mokasa/Jagir assignments within Maratha territory granted revenue rights to sardars but did not create autonomous political authority
statement_analysis.reason: Mokasa/Jagir assignments did in practice create semi-autonomous power centres; sardars who accumulated large Mokasa assignments exercised significant independent political and military authority, contributing to confederacy fragmentation.

statement_analysis.statement: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were original innovations of the Peshwa period — Shivaji's administration did not use these instruments
statement_analysis.reason: Both Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were innovations of Shivaji himself; the Peshwa period massively expanded their geographic scope but did not originate the instruments.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify the first two pairs but are uncertain about Statement 3 may assume Mokasa did not create political authority (since it was formally a revenue assignment), pushing them toward three correct pairings.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Chauth as 1/4th of revenue is a fixed fact; this is correct.
Verify Statement 2 — Sardeshmukhi as 10% hereditary claim over Deccan is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Mokasa/Jagir in practice did create autonomous power centres (Holkar, Scindia arose this way); the claim that it did NOT create autonomy is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Both taxes originated under Shivaji, not the Peshwas; this is incorrect.
Only two statements (1 and 2) are correct — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the most dangerous trap: students who know the Peshwa period expanded Chauth/Sardeshmukhi collection may leap to attributing the instruments' origin to the Peshwas. The question is designed so that a student recalling 'Peshwa period expanded Chauth' without precision about origin will mark Statement 4 as correct, inflating the count to three. Statement 3's trap works by appealing to the formal definition of Mokasa (revenue assignment) while ignoring its practical political consequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha revenue system rested on two key extraterritorial levies — Chauth and Sardeshmukhi — both of which originated under Shivaji and were expanded geographically during the Peshwa period.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Chauth was 1/4th of assessed revenue as a protection levy, not implying direct administration.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10%, claimed as a hereditary right of the Maratha chief as Sardeshmukh (senior headman) of the Deccan.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Mokasa/Jagir assignments in practice created semi-autonomous power centres. Holkar and Scindia are prime examples of sardars whose Mokasa holdings gave them independent political and military standing.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Both taxes were Shivaji's innovations. The Peshwa period expanded their geographic scope dramatically — into Malwa, Gujarat, Bengal — but did not originate them.

Value Addition:
• Chauth and Sardeshmukhi together amounted to 35% of revenue from non-Maratha territories.
• The Mokasa system's autonomy problem was a structural weakness that contributed to the lack of unified command at Panipat III.
• Sardeshmukhi was claimed specifically over the Deccan; Chauth was extracted from a much wider geography.

solution.concept_anchor: Five Maratha confederacy houses and their territories
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) swaps Holkar and Scindia's capitals (Indore and Gwalior), which many students confuse because both are in central India and both houses were powerful military sardars.
elimination_logic: Confirm A-3: Peshwa's seat was Pune — this is an anchor match students can lock in first.
Confirm D-1: Gaekwad controlled Gujarat with Baroda as their base — another relatively known pairing.
Distinguish B and C: Holkar is associated with Indore and Scindia with Gwalior — the geographic-swap trap places these reversed in option (a); Holkar=Indore (B-4) and Scindia=Gwalior (C-2).
The only option consistent with A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Holkar-Scindia geographic swap is a classic UPSC-style trap. Both families operated in central India, both are associated with military power, and students who have not precisely memorised Holkar=Indore and Scindia=Gwalior will often reverse them. Option (a) exploits this by reversing exactly these two pairings while keeping the other two correct, making it appear plausible to a partially prepared student.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha Confederacy was a loose alliance of five major houses, each controlling distinct territories while nominally acknowledging the Peshwa's leadership.

Correct pairings:
• A (Peshwa) — 3 (Pune): The Peshwa's political and administrative headquarters was Pune (Poona), which grew into a major political and cultural centre.
• B (Holkar) — 4 (Indore): The Holkar family controlled the Malwa region with Indore as their principal seat.
• C (Scindia) — 2 (Gwalior): The Scindia (Shinde) family established dominance in northern Malwa and Rajputana, with Gwalior as their stronghold.
• D (Gaekwad) — 1 (Baroda): The Gaekwad family administered Gujarat with their seat at Baroda.

The Bhonsle of Nagpur are the fifth major house (not listed here) — important for the Bengal connection.

Trap: Options (a) and (b) reverse Holkar and Scindia's territorial associations — the most commonly confused pairing.

Value Addition:
• The Gaekwad were technically subordinate to the Peshwa but exercised considerable autonomy in Gujarat.
• Scindia's Gwalior became strategically critical during the Anglo-Maratha Wars.
• The confederacy's loose structure meant each chief pursued independent foreign policy, undermining collective Maratha strength.

solution.concept_anchor: Baji Rao I's 1737 Delhi raid — demonstration not conquest
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and the causal link sounds superficially plausible — students may assume that reaching Delhi's vicinity naturally translates into a territorial demonstration, making R appear to explain A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Baji Rao I's forces reached the outskirts of Delhi in 1737, causing alarm at the Mughal court. This is historically verified.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Baji Rao I never formally captured or administered Delhi; the campaign was a cavalry demonstration of power, not a territorial annexation.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. A states that the campaign was a psychological blow to Mughal prestige; R states that Delhi was not captured. These are two independent factual observations — R describes what did NOT happen, while A describes a psychological consequence. The reason for the psychological impact was the reach of Maratha cavalry to the Mughal heartland, not the absence of formal capture. R does not explain WHY A was a psychological blow; it merely adds a separate fact.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This assertion-reason is designed so that both A and R are true but causally disconnected. Students who read quickly will see 'A true, R true' and select option (a). The question tests whether the student understands that R (Delhi was not captured) is a separate fact from A (it was a psychological blow). The blow to Mughal prestige came from Maratha cavalry reaching Delhi's vicinity — an event so audacious that it shook the empire's self-image. The fact that no formal conquest occurred is an independent observation, not the explanation for the psychological impact.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao I's northern campaigns culminated in a dramatic cavalry raid that brought Maratha forces to the outskirts of Delhi in 1737 — an event unprecedented in the post-Aurangzeb era.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Maratha forces' appearance near the Mughal capital in 1737 was a profound psychological blow — the Mughals, already weakened, could not prevent Maratha cavalry from reaching the heart of their empire.
• Reason (R): Correct. Baji Rao I's campaign was a demonstration of military reach, not a bid for administrative control. Delhi was never formally captured or administered by the Marathas.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The psychological damage to Mughal prestige arose from the sheer audacity of Maratha forces reaching Delhi — not from the absence of formal capture. R describes what did not happen; A describes the psychological consequence of what did happen. They are independent factual claims.

Value Addition:
• After the 1737 raid, Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah invited Nadir Shah for help — ironically, Nadir Shah's 1739 invasion was far more destructive.
• Baji Rao's northern campaigns are considered the high watermark of early Peshwa military power.
• The 1738 Treaty of Bhopal, which followed this phase, gave Marathas formal control of Malwa.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of major Maratha-Mughal agreements and battles
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the Treaty of Bhopal before the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon, which seems plausible to students who remember only that both involved the Nizam and Maratha expansion but have not fixed the precise dates.
elimination_logic: Anchor the 1719 Maratha-Mughal treaty (Sayyid Brothers) as the earliest event — before Baji Rao I's campaigns even began.
Place Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon next — it followed the Battle of Palkhed in 1728.
Treaty of Bhopal followed the Battle of Bhopal in 1738 — after Mungi-Shegaon.
Battle of Udgir (1760) is the latest event — just before Panipat III; correct sequence is 1→3→2→4, which is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often confuse Mungi-Shegaon (1728) and Bhopal (1738) because both involve the Nizam as a party. Options (b) and (c) exploit this by reversing their order. The 1719 treaty is the anchor that most students can place correctly; the challenge is ordering the two Nizam-related agreements and placing Udgir last. A student with only approximate knowledge will struggle to distinguish 1728 from 1738 and may default to an incorrect sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
Ordering these four agreements reveals the progressive arc of Maratha power from revenue rights (1719) to territorial sovereignty (1738) to regional dominance (1760).

Correct sequence: 1719 Treaty → Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon (1728) → Treaty of Bhopal (1738) → Battle of Udgir (1760)

• 1719 Maratha-Mughal Treaty: First, brokered through Sayyid Brothers — granted revenue rights over Deccan, released Shahu.
• Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon (1728): Second, following Palkhed — Nizam acknowledged Maratha Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights in Deccan.
• Treaty of Bhopal (1738): Third, following Baji Rao I's northern campaigns — Mughals formally ceded Malwa, a qualitative territorial leap.
• Battle of Udgir (1760): Last, decisive Maratha victory over the Nizam just before Panipat III — Nizam ceded Bidar and surrounding territories.

Value Addition:
• Each agreement marks a distinct stage: fiscal recognition → Deccan hegemony → territorial sovereignty → regional supremacy.
• Udgir (1760) is frequently overlooked because it occurred just before Panipat III (1761).
• The 1719 treaty is the only one involving Mughal imperial authority directly; later agreements were with the Nizam as a regional power.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha Bargi raids — tribute extraction vs territorial conquest
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'territorial annexation' is a strong distractor because students who know the Marathas reached Bengal and extracted significant concessions (Orissa cession, Chauth agreement) may assume this constitutes territorial expansion of the Maratha state.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — diplomatic alliance implies mutual benefit and formal cooperation; the Bargi raids were coercive, not cooperative.
Eliminate option (c) — territorial annexation requires administrative control; Marathas never administered Bengal, and the raids were about tribute extraction.
Eliminate option (d) — punitive expedition implies a response to a prior attack; Maratha raids into Bengal were proactive revenue-seeking operations.
Confirm option (b) — the raids fit the model of tributary extraction through military intimidation, consistent with the Maratha Chauth system extended eastward.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Orissa cession in the 1751 treaty tempts students into selecting 'territorial annexation'. While Orissa was ceded, this was a specific concession within a tribute-framework negotiation — the Marathas did not administer Bengal and the primary objective was Chauth extraction. Option (c) is precisely calibrated to attract students who remember 'Orissa cession' without understanding its nature within the broader tributary relationship.
solution.final_explanation:
Between 1741 and 1751, Maratha light cavalry (Bargis) conducted repeated raids into Bengal under the Peshwaship of Balaji Baji Rao. The Bengal Nawab Alivardi Khan resisted militarily but eventually negotiated.

The operative principle here is tributary extraction: Marathas used military pressure not to annex and administer territory, but to extract Chauth payments and other concessions. This mirrors their approach in Malwa, Gujarat, and Rajputana — presence without administration.

• Option (a) — diplomatic alliance: Incorrect. The relationship was coercive, not cooperative; Alivardi Khan fought the Bargis militarily before accepting terms.
• Option (b) — tributary extraction through military intimidation: Correct. The 1751 treaty extracted Chauth for Bengal and the cession of Orissa — classic Maratha revenue logic applied eastward.
• Option (c) — territorial annexation: Incorrect. Marathas never established administrative control over Bengal. The raids were economically motivated incursions.
• Option (d) — punitive expedition: Incorrect. This implies retaliation; the Bargi raids were offensive revenue-seeking operations.

Value Addition:
• The Bargi raids entered Bengali folk memory as a traumatic period; lullabies about 'Bargis coming' survived into the 19th century.
• Alivardi Khan's inability to defeat the Marathas permanently revealed the weakness of Bengal's military at this time.
• The 1751 Orissa cession gave Marathas formal revenue rights in eastern India.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Udgir — Maratha triumph before Panipat III
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) Battle of Bhopal is a strong distractor because it also involved the Nizam and is a significant Maratha military event; students may group it with Palkhed and Udgir as Nizam-conflicts and fail to notice it belongs to that same set, making them doubt Panipat III as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: Palkhed (1728), Bhopal (1738), and Udgir (1760) all involved direct Maratha military conflict against the Nizam-ul-Mulk.

Evaluate Panipat III (1761): This was fought against Ahmad Shah Abdali's coalition — the Nizam was not the opponent; in fact, the Nizam was part of the anti-Maratha environment but not a direct combatant at Panipat.
Confirm: Panipat III does NOT belong to the category of Maratha-Nizam conflicts.
Answer is (c) — Third Battle of Panipat.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know that the Nizam repeatedly opposed the Marathas may assume all four listed battles involve the Nizam and struggle to identify the odd one out. The trap is that Panipat III (1761) is a Maratha defeat against the Durrani/Afghan coalition — not a Nizam-Maratha conflict. A student who remembers only that all four battles are 18th-century Maratha military events without anchoring the opponents will likely pick incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha-Nizam rivalry produced several decisive military encounters over three decades.

• Battle of Palkhed (1728): Maratha victory over Nizam-ul-Mulk — belongs to the Nizam-conflict series.
• Battle of Bhopal (1738): Maratha victory over Nizam-backed Mughal forces — belongs to the Nizam-conflict series.
• Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Maratha defeat against Ahmad Shah Abdali's coalition (Rohilla Afghans + Awadh Nawab) — the Nizam was not the primary opponent. This is the odd one out.
• Battle of Udgir (1760): Decisive Maratha victory over the Nizam — belongs to the Nizam-conflict series.

Value Addition:
• Udgir (1760) was the last major Maratha victory before Panipat III — making it particularly ironic that the greatest triumph was followed within a year by the greatest disaster.
• At Panipat III, the Nizam remained neutral — he did not join Abdali's coalition but also did not help the Marathas.
• The three Nizam-conflict victories (Palkhed, Bhopal, Udgir) together cemented Maratha dominance in the Deccan.

strong_distractor: b — Option (b) Battle of Udgir is a strong distractor because students who know it occurred just before Panipat III may associate it with the Panipat context rather than the Nizam-conflict series.

solution.concept_anchor: Panipat III — Abdali's Indian coalition partners
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) Mir Qasim is a strong distractor because he was a prominent anti-British 18th-century Muslim ruler in northern India, and students may confuse his Buxar context with the Panipat context.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Mir Qasim — he was the Bengal Nawab who fought the British at the Battle of Buxar (1764); he had no role in the Panipat III coalition.
Eliminate Hyder Ali — he was the Mysore ruler who was a Maratha rival in the south but was not part of Abdali's northern coalition.
Eliminate Suraj Mal — the Jat chief of Bharatpur who actually withdrew from the Maratha camp before the battle; he was an ally who deserted, not an opponent.
Confirm Shuja-ud-Daula — the Nawab of Awadh who joined Abdali's coalition along with Najib-ud-Daula's Rohilla Afghans.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students preparing Panipat III know Abdali and Najib-ud-Daula but frequently forget Shuja-ud-Daula (Awadh) as the third major coalition partner. Option (c) Mir Qasim is deliberately placed as a plausible 18th-century Muslim ruler who fought in northern India — but he fought the British at Buxar (1764), not the Marathas at Panipat (1761). This temporal and contextual confusion is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was not merely a Maratha-Afghan confrontation; it involved a coalition of anti-Maratha powers.

• Option (a) — Hyder Ali: Incorrect. Hyder Ali was the Mysore sultan and a Maratha rival in the south, but he was not part of Abdali's Panipat coalition.
• Option (b) — Shuja-ud-Daula: Correct. The Nawab of Awadh joined Ahmad Shah Abdali's coalition alongside Najib-ud-Daula's Rohillas, forming the combined force that defeated the Marathas.
• Option (c) — Mir Qasim: Incorrect. He was the Nawab of Bengal who later fought the British at the Battle of Buxar (1764) — a different conflict, different adversary, different context.
• Option (d) — Suraj Mal: Incorrect. The Jat chief of Bharatpur was initially with the Maratha camp but withdrew before the battle due to disagreements — he was a defector, not a coalition opponent.

Value Addition:
• The Panipat III coalition succeeded partly because the Marathas had alienated potential allies like the Jats and Rajputs through arrogant treatment.
• Abdali withdrew from India after his victory — he had no intention of establishing permanent rule.
• The battle is described in contemporary accounts as one of the bloodiest single-day engagements in South Asian history.

solution.concept_anchor: Madhav Rao I — post-Panipat revival and early death
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Baji Rao I also defeated Hyder Ali's predecessor-context forces and is associated with southern campaigns; students may assign Madhav Rao I's specific southern victories to Baji Rao I.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b) — Baji Rao I's tenure was 1720–1740; Hyder Ali rose to prominence in the 1760s, long after Baji Rao I's death. Baji Rao I could not have checked Hyder Ali.
Eliminate option (c) — Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) died shortly after Panipat III (1761); the revival of Maratha power occurred under his successor Madhav Rao I (1761–1772).
Eliminate option (d) — Raghunathrao (Raghoba) is associated with the succession crisis and the Surat Treaty (1775), not post-Panipat military revival.
Confirm option (a) — Madhav Rao I (1761–1772) defeated Hyder Ali twice and re-established Maratha influence across Rajputana and the south before his early death.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Madhav Rao I is a chronologically underappreciated Peshwa. Students focus on Baji Rao I (military genius) and Balaji Baji Rao (expansionist peak) and skip over Madhav Rao I's crucial 11-year revival. Option (b) exploits this by attributing Madhav Rao I's achievement of checking Hyder Ali to the more famous Baji Rao I — a temporal impossibility that a rushed student may overlook.
solution.final_explanation:
Following the catastrophe of Panipat III (1761), the Maratha empire required urgent reconstruction — and Madhav Rao I delivered it within a remarkably short period.

• Option (a): Correctly matched. Madhav Rao I (Peshwa 1761–1772) defeated Hyder Ali of Mysore in 1764 and 1767, re-established Maratha tributary authority over Rajput states, and restored Maratha prestige across India — all within 11 years before his death at 27.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Baji Rao I's tenure (1720–1740) predates Hyder Ali's rise; attributing the containment of Hyder Ali to Baji Rao I is a temporal impossibility.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Balaji Baji Rao died shortly after receiving news of Panipat III; the revival occurred under his successor.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Raghunathrao is associated with the succession crisis of the 1770s and the Surat Treaty (1775), not military revival.

Value Addition:
• Madhav Rao I's early death at 27 (from tuberculosis, 1772) is considered one of the greatest 'what if' moments in Maratha history.
• His reign represents the only successful post-Panipat recovery — subsequent Peshwas could not replicate it.
• The conflict with Raghoba (his uncle) throughout his reign consumed administrative energy that could have been directed outward.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Surat vs Treaty of Salbai — distinct agreements

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Surat (1775) involved Raghunathrao ceding Salsette and Broach to the British East India Company in exchange for military support for his claim to the Peshwaship.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise content of the 1775 Surat Treaty — Raghoba exchanged territorial concessions (Salsette and Broach) for British armed backing of his succession claim.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored all territories taken during the First Anglo-Maratha War to Maratha control, including Salsette.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Salbai preserved British possession of Salsette — it was effectively a status quo ante agreement on other matters; Salsette was not returned to the Marathas.

statement_analysis.statement: The Maratha Puna court's rejection of the Surat Treaty's terms was a direct cause of the First Anglo-Maratha War.
statement_analysis.reason: The Puna court (acting regency for infant Peshwa Madhavrao II) repudiated the Surat Treaty as unauthorised by the legitimate Maratha authority — this repudiation, combined with British military moves, triggered the war.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know both treaties may assume all three statements are broadly true and select 'all correct', especially if they are uncertain about the specific Salsette clause in the Salbai Treaty.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Surat Treaty (1775): Salsette + Broach ceded in exchange for British support for Raghoba; this is textbook content.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Salbai (1782) is described as 'status quo ante' but British retained Salsette; the statement claiming ALL territories were returned, including Salsette, is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — The Puna court's repudiation of Surat Treaty as unauthorised triggered the First Anglo-Maratha War; this is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Salbai Treaty's Salsette retention is a precision trap. Students who remember 'Salbai = status quo ante bellum' may assume this means everything was restored to the pre-war position, including Salsette. However, the British retained Salsette under Salbai — the 'status quo' related to other territorial acquisitions, not Salsette. This detail separates students with precise knowledge from those with approximate knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The Raghoba crisis initiated a complex chain of events that drew the British East India Company into internal Maratha politics for the first time.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Raghoba (Raghunathrao) signed the Treaty of Surat (1775) ceding Salsette and Broach to the Bombay Presidency in exchange for British troops to support his Peshwaship claim.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) did not restore all wartime territorial changes. Significantly, Salsette remained with the British. The treaty was broadly a status quo arrangement on other contested areas, but British retention of Salsette was a lasting outcome of this period.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Puna regency (acting for infant Peshwa Madhavrao II / Sawai Madhavrao) refused to recognise the Surat Treaty as binding, since Raghoba had no authority to cede Maratha territory. This repudiation was a proximate cause of the First Anglo-Maratha War.

Value Addition:
• The Battle of Wadgaon (1779) during the First Anglo-Maratha War was a rare British military defeat; the Convention of Wadgaon humiliated the Bombay army.
• Warren Hastings repudiated the Convention of Wadgaon and reorganised the British strategy — ultimately leading to Salbai.
• The 20-year peace clause in Salbai delayed the Second Anglo-Maratha War until 1803.

solution.concept_anchor: Nana Fadnavis — 'last of the Marathas' and death 1800
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because Madhav Rao I's death (1772) was also a critical turning point, and students may associate 'end of effective Maratha governance' with his death rather than Nana Fadnavis's.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Baji Rao II became Peshwa in 1796; the question asks about Nana Fadnavis specifically.
Eliminate option (c) — The Battle of Kharda (1795) was a Maratha victory over the Nizam; while significant, it is not the event associated with Nana's death or the 'last of Marathas' description.
Eliminate option (d) — Madhav Rao I died in 1772; Nana Fadnavis remained active through the 1790s as a political manager.
Confirm option (b) — Nana Fadnavis died in 1800, and his death directly preceded the Second Anglo-Maratha War; he is described as 'the last of the Marathas' in historical accounts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) deliberately places Madhav Rao I as the turning point, exploiting the fact that his death (1772) was genuinely significant. Students who know Madhav Rao I's importance but have not specifically studied Nana Fadnavis's death year (1800) and its consequences will gravitate toward (d). The 'last of the Marathas' designation for Nana Fadnavis is a specific historical characterisation that rewards precise reading.
solution.final_explanation:
Nana Fadnavis was the most effective political manager of the late Peshwa period — he operated without a formal military command but held the Maratha confederacy together through diplomatic skill.

• Option (a) — Ascension of Baji Rao II: Incorrect. Baji Rao II became Peshwa in 1796 after Sawai Madhavrao's death; Nana Fadnavis survived into his reign but the question asks what directly preceded the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
• Option (b) — Death of Nana Fadnavis in 1800: Correct. His death removed the last effective Maratha political intelligence from the scene. The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) followed directly, and without Nana's diplomatic balancing, the confederacy could not resist British pressure.
• Option (c) — Battle of Kharda (1795): Incorrect. Though significant, Kharda was a Maratha victory over the Nizam — it does not directly connect to the 'last of the Marathas' designation.
• Option (d) — Death of Madhav Rao I (1772): Incorrect. This was significant for Maratha revival prospects, but Nana Fadnavis then managed affairs effectively through the 1780s and 1790s.

Value Addition:
• Nana Fadnavis served under four successive Peshwas as the effective power behind the throne.
• He attempted a Triple Alliance (Marathas, Hyderabad, Mysore) against British — it collapsed due to mutual suspicion.
• Arthur Wellesley (future Duke of Wellington) described Nana Fadnavis as 'the last of the Marathas' after his death.

solution.concept_anchor: Marathas as first major challengers to Hyder Ali — not British

statement_analysis.statement: The British East India Company was the primary power to first militarily challenge Hyder Ali's expansion in Karnataka and Mysore before the Maratha campaigns under Madhav Rao I.
statement_analysis.reason: The Marathas under Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali in 1764 and 1767 — well before the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–1769); Marathas, not the British, were the first major military challenge to Hyder Ali.

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Rakshasbhuvan (1763) was a Maratha victory over the Nizam in the Marathwada region, preceding the southern campaigns.
statement_analysis.reason: Rakshasbhuvan (1763) was indeed a Maratha victory over the Nizam — it consolidated Maratha power in Marathwada before Madhav Rao I turned his attention southward.

statement_analysis.statement: Madhav Rao I's campaigns against Hyder Ali were motivated primarily by religious considerations rather than territorial and revenue interests.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhav Rao I's campaigns against Hyder Ali were driven by geopolitical and revenue interests — checking Mysore's expansion into Karnataka, which overlapped with Maratha tributary claims — not by religious motivation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) — identifying only Statement 3 as incorrect — is a strong distractor because Statement 3's attribution of religious motivation is clearly wrong to most students, leading them to accept it as the sole incorrect item without scrutinising Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — First Anglo-Mysore War was 1767–1769; Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali in 1764 — Marathas preceded British militarily against Hyder Ali. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Rakshasbhuvan (1763) as a Maratha-Nizam battle in Marathwada is historically accurate. Statement 2 is correct — not an answer.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Maratha campaigns were geopolitical/revenue driven, not religiously motivated. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the dominant Anglo-Mysore Wars narrative. Students taught primarily through the lens of British expansion tend to associate Hyder Ali's first major military challenges with the Anglo-Mysore Wars. The Maratha campaigns against Hyder Ali (1764, 1767) predate the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–1769) and are structurally overlooked. A student who knows only the British-Hyder Ali context will accept Statement 1 as correct, missing the central trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Maratha southern expansion under Madhav Rao I is a frequently underemphasised aspect of Peshwa-period history, overshadowed by the more studied Anglo-Mysore Wars.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali in 1764 and again in 1767, making the Marathas the first major power to militarily check his Karnataka expansion — predating the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–1769).
• Statement 2 — Correct: Rakshasbhuvan (1763) was a Maratha victory over the Nizam in Marathwada — accurately described and correctly placed before the southern campaigns.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Maratha interests in Karnataka were territorial and tributary — protecting Chauth collection zones and checking the growth of a rival power. Framing this as religiously motivated misrepresents Maratha strategic logic.

Value Addition:
• The Maratha-Mysore rivalry for Karnataka is a distinct chapter from the British-Mysore conflict, though both overlap chronologically.
• Hyder Ali's son Tipu Sultan later became the primary adversary of both Marathas and British.
• Madhav Rao I's check on Hyder Ali temporarily limited Mysore's northern expansion — after Madhav Rao's death (1772), Hyder Ali resumed expansion.

solution.concept_anchor: Sawai Madhavrao death 1795 — functional end of Peshwa governance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct and the logical link seems tight: Nana Fadnavis managed affairs under Sawai Madhavrao, and his death caused a succession crisis — making R appear to explain A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Sawai Madhavrao's reign was conducted under Nana Fadnavis's effective management; the Peshwa was nominal while Nana held real authority.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Sawai Madhavrao died in 1795 (by suicide), and his death did trigger the final succession crisis that brought Baji Rao II to power, marking the effective end of Peshwa governance.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R explains the consequence of Sawai Madhavrao's tenure ending, not the reason why his governance was nominal. His nominal authority existed because Nana Fadnavis managed affairs — not because he later died in 1795. The death and succession crisis (R) is a temporal consequence, not a causal explanation for the nominal nature of his authority (A).
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is a temporal confusion masquerading as causation. R (Sawai Madhavrao's death triggering succession crisis) is a consequence that came AFTER the nominal governance described in A. Students who read quickly will see 'nominal authority → death → succession crisis' as a logical progression and select (a). The question tests whether students recognise that the explanation for A (nominal authority under Nana Fadnavis) is the regency structure — not the subsequent death event.
solution.final_explanation:
Sawai Madhavrao (Madhavrao II, Peshwa 1774–1795) represents the structural repetition of the Chhatrapati-Peshwa dynamic at a lower level: a nominal titleholder with a powerful de facto manager (Nana Fadnavis).

• Assertion (A): Correct. Sawai Madhavrao's reign was conducted under Nana Fadnavis's regency — real decisions on diplomacy, military strategy, and internal politics were Nana's. The Peshwa's authority was ceremonial in practice.
• Reason (R): Correct. Sawai Madhavrao died in 1795 (suicide), triggering the final succession dispute that elevated Baji Rao II — Raghoba's son — to the Peshwaship, marking the functional end of effective Peshwa governance.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The nominal nature of Sawai Madhavrao's authority was a consequence of the regency structure and Nana Fadnavis's political dominance — established from the beginning of his reign. R describes what happened at the end of his reign, not why his authority was nominal throughout.

Value Addition:
• The Chhatrapati-Peshwa dynamic and Peshwa-Nana dynamic are structural parallels — nominal vs. real authority repeating at different institutional levels.
• Baji Rao II (who followed) is associated with the final collapse; his Peshwaship is studied under the Anglo-Maratha Wars phase.
• Sawai Madhavrao's reign (1774–1795) still saw significant Maratha military activity, partly because Nana Fadnavis was an effective strategist.

solution.concept_anchor: Panipat III — causes and consequences

statement_analysis.statement: One contributing factor to the Maratha defeat at Panipat III was the alienation of potential Rajput and Jat allies due to Maratha demands and treatment of these powers.
statement_analysis.reason: Historical accounts confirm that Maratha overconfidence and extractive demands alienated the Rajput states and the Jat chief Suraj Mal, who withdrew before the battle — leaving the Marathas without crucial allied support.

statement_analysis.statement: Ahmad Shah Abdali permanently established Afghan political authority over the Punjab and Delhi following his victory at Panipat III.
statement_analysis.reason: Abdali withdrew from India after the victory without establishing permanent Afghan rule; the Punjab was left under a subordinate and Delhi remained under nominal Mughal authority — the British, not Afghans, were the eventual beneficiaries of the Maratha collapse.

statement_analysis.statement: The collapse of Maratha supply lines during the Panipat III campaign was a significant military factor that weakened their position before the decisive engagement.
statement_analysis.reason: The Maratha force, deep in northern India, faced severe supply shortages; Abdali's forces cut off provisioning routes, exhausting Maratha troops before the main battle even began.

statement_analysis.statement: The long-term consequence most frequently asked about in competitive examinations is that the British East India Company was the principal power to benefit from the Maratha defeat at Panipat III.
statement_analysis.reason: Panipat III eliminated the one power capable of replacing the Mughals as a pan-Indian authority; the resulting power vacuum was ultimately filled by the British — a standard UPSC question formulation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor that is also the correct answer; students may overcorrect by accepting Statement 2 as partially true (Abdali did control Punjab briefly) and marking all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — alienation of Rajputs and Jats is a documented Panipat III cause; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Abdali withdrew from India without permanent establishment; he left a subordinate in Punjab but did not create permanent Afghan empire. This statement is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — supply line collapse is a textbook Panipat III military factor; correct.
Confirm Statement 4 — British as the principal beneficiary of Panipat III is a standard UPSC analytical point; correct.
Three statements correct (1, 3, 4) → option (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the precision trap: Abdali did exercise influence over Punjab for a period, and a student who recalls 'Abdali controlled Punjab' may mark this as correct. The key distinction is 'permanently established Afghan political authority' — he did not. Abdali's withdrawal without administrative consolidation is a standard examination point. Students who know 'Abdali won Panipat' but lack the follow-through detail of his withdrawal will accept the 'permanent establishment' claim.
solution.final_explanation:
Panipat III (1761) is one of the most consequential battles in South Asian history — its causes and consequences are standard examination material.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rajput states and Jat chief Suraj Mal withdrew from Maratha alliance partly due to Maratha arrogance and extractive demands — a classic lesson in alliance management failure.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Abdali departed India after the victory. He installed a subordinate in Punjab but never created a permanent Afghan empire in India. The principal long-term beneficiary was the British East India Company.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Maratha supply lines were cut by Abdali's forces; troops deep in the northern plains faced starvation conditions before the decisive engagement — a material military disadvantage.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Maratha defeat eliminated the one successor power capable of pan-Indian empire; the resulting vacuum was gradually filled by British expansion — frequently asked as 'who benefited most from Panipat III?'

Value Addition:
• Vishwasrao (Viswasrao) and Bhausaheb's deaths at Panipat created an enormous leadership vacuum.
• The 'emptying of Maharashtra' refers to the loss of virtually an entire generation of Maratha nobility.
• Abdali's withdrawal pattern (raid, win, leave) is distinct from earlier conquerors who established permanent rule.

solution.concept_anchor: Confederacy fragmentation — sardars' autonomous power from Mokasa/Jagir
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students know the Peshwa was the nominal head of the confederacy and may assume any resistance from sardars constitutes a challenge to Mughal authority rather than an internal confederacy tension.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — the scenario describes internal Maratha confederacy tension, not a Maratha-British conflict; British authority is not relevant here.
Eliminate option (b) — the sardar is defying the Peshwa's directive, not asserting Maratha identity against Mughal claims; Mughal suzerainty is not the issue.
Eliminate option (c) — religious autonomy is not what the scenario describes; the sardar's independence is revenue-military, not religious.

Confirm option (d) — the scenario precisely illustrates the Mokasa/Jagir system creating autonomous power centres, with sardars leveraging revenue assignments to act independently of the Peshwa — the structural weakness that contributed to confederacy fragmentation and Panipat III.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) sounds plausible because students associate Maratha sardars with resistance to external powers. The scenario, however, describes internal confederacy tension — the sardar defying the Peshwa, not a foreign power. Students who read quickly and associate 'sardar refusing orders' with 'Maratha resistance to Mughals' will pick (b) without registering that the authority being defied is the Peshwa, not the Mughal emperor.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha Confederacy's structural weakness was that revenue assignments (Mokasa/Jagir) to sardars created semi-autonomous power bases that could defy central Peshwa authority.

Applicable principle: The Mokasa/Jagir system within Maratha-controlled territory granted sardars revenue rights that, when large enough, translated into military and political autonomy. This is precisely what enabled Holkar, Scindia, Bhonsle (Nagpur), and Gaekwad to act as near-independent rulers while nominally acknowledging the Peshwa.

Mapping to the scenario: The sardar controls significant revenue from his Mokasa assignment, has built his own military force, and refuses the Peshwa's deployment order — a textbook illustration of how revenue autonomy becomes political autonomy.

• Option (a) — British encroachment on Maratha sovereignty: Incorrect. The British are not mentioned or implied; this is an intra-Maratha dispute.
• Option (b) — Maratha sardar asserting collective Maratha identity against Mughal suzerainty: Incorrect. The defiance is directed at the Peshwa, not the Mughals.
• Option (c) — religious autonomy of regional chiefs: Incorrect. The scenario is about revenue-military independence, not religious practice.
• Option (d) — Mokasa/Jagir system creating autonomous power centres: Correct. This is the structural explanation for sardar independence.

Value Addition:
• This structural problem was identified by historians as a primary reason for the lack of unified command at Panipat III.
• The Holkar-Scindia rivalry within the confederacy is a later manifestation of the same problem.
• The Peshwa's authority over sardars was always negotiated, never absolute.

solution.concept_anchor: Hindu Pad Padshahi — ideology vs military reality

statement_analysis.statement: Baji Rao I's concept of 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' envisioned Maratha political authority replacing Mughal suzerainty as the paramount power across the Indian subcontinent.
statement_analysis.reason: Hindu Pad Padshahi was Baji Rao I's stated political ideology — Maratha paramountcy over all India — a vision that informed his northern campaigns toward Delhi, Rajputana, and Bundelkhand.

statement_analysis.statement: Baji Rao I's alliance with Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand was purely military, with no political or dynastic dimension linking the two powers.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chhatrasal alliance was explicitly political and dynastic — Chhatrasal bequeathed part of his territory to Baji Rao I, and Mastani (Baji Rao I's second consort) was Chhatrasal's daughter, cementing a personal-political bond beyond mere military cooperation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both statements seem broadly accurate when read quickly — the Hindu Pad Padshahi ideology is well-known, and students aware of the Chhatrasal alliance may not recall the Mastani/dynastic detail.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Hindu Pad Padshahi as a pan-Indian Maratha paramountcy ideology is a documented and well-attested concept associated with Baji Rao I; this is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2 — The claim 'purely military, no dynastic dimension' is factually false; Mastani was Chhatrasal's daughter, making the alliance explicitly personal-dynastic, and territorial cession was part of the agreement.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
Correct answer is (c) — Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is the word 'purely' — a scope-extension qualifier that makes an otherwise recognisable fact (Chhatrasal-Baji Rao alliance) into a false claim. Students who recall 'military alliance' without the Mastani detail will accept Statement 2 as broadly correct. The Mastani connection transforms the alliance from a military arrangement into a dynastic political entanglement — the word 'purely' is the pivot.
solution.final_explanation:
Baji Rao I's northern campaigns combined military ambition with a coherent political ideology and sophisticated alliance-building.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Hindu Pad Padshahi (literally 'Hindu paramount sovereignty') articulated Baji Rao I's vision of Maratha suzerainty replacing Mughal supremacy as the governing principle of Indian political order. This ideology informed his campaigns into Malwa, Rajputana, Bundelkhand, and toward Delhi.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Chhatrasal alliance was deeply political and dynastic. Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand requested Maratha military aid against Mughal pressure; in gratitude, he ceded a portion of Bundelkhand to Baji Rao I and his daughter Mastani became Baji Rao I's second consort. This Mastani episode created significant controversy in Pune's orthodox Brahmin circles, demonstrating the alliance's profound personal-political dimension.

Value Addition:
• Mastani's controversial status (as a Muslim-origin consort of the Brahmin Peshwa) created a political crisis in Pune.
• Chhatrasal's cession of territory brought Jhansi under Maratha influence — later significant in the 1857 context.
• Hindu Pad Padshahi as an ideology had limits: Baji Rao I sought Maratha supremacy, not elimination of all non-Hindu powers.

solution.concept_anchor: Sardeshmukhi — hereditary claim distinct from Chauth
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) conflates Chauth and Sardeshmukhi as equivalent protection taxes collected from the same territories on the same basis, which is incorrect; Sardeshmukhi was a separate, additional levy with a distinct legal justification.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b) — Sardeshmukhi and Chauth were not the same tax; Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% on top of Chauth, claimed on a different legal basis.
Eliminate option (c) — Sardeshmukhi was not a tax on trade routes; it was a land revenue levy claimed by virtue of the Maratha chief's position as Sardeshmukh.
Eliminate option (d) — Sardeshmukhi was not limited to territories directly administered by Marathas; like Chauth, it was extracted from non-Maratha areas.
Confirm option (a) — Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% of revenue claimed by the Maratha chief as hereditary senior headman (Sardeshmukh) of the Deccan, over and above the Chauth.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is calibrated to attract students who know Sardeshmukhi involves revenue extraction but confuse its legal basis and percentage with Chauth. Chauth was the 'protection' levy (1/4th); Sardeshmukhi was a 'hereditary headman' levy (1/10th). The percentage difference and the distinct legal justification are the precise knowledge tested here. Students who remember 'Sardeshmukhi = revenue tax = similar to Chauth' without the specific percentage or hereditary justification will select (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Sardeshmukhi was a conceptually distinct levy from Chauth, though both were extracted from non-Maratha territories.

• Option (a): Correct. Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% of revenue claimed by the Maratha chief on the basis of being the hereditary Sardeshmukh (senior headman) of the Deccan — a traditional right asserted by Shivaji and expanded during the Peshwa period.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Sardeshmukhi and Chauth were not equivalent; Chauth was 25% as a protection levy while Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% based on a hereditary claim — different percentages and different legal justifications.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Sardeshmukhi was not a trade route tax; it applied to assessed land revenue.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Sardeshmukhi, like Chauth, was extracted from territories not under direct Maratha administration — it was an extraterritorial claim, not limited to directly governed areas.

Value Addition:
• Together, Chauth (25%) + Sardeshmukhi (10%) = 35% of assessed revenue extracted from non-Maratha territories.
• The Sardeshmukhi claim was specifically over the Deccan; Chauth was extracted from a much wider geography.
• Both levies were granted formal Mughal recognition in the 1719 treaty — a milestone in Maratha legitimacy.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Wadgaon — British defeat and Convention

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Wadgaon (1779) during the First Anglo-Maratha War resulted in a significant defeat for the British Bombay army, leading to the Convention of Wadgaon.
statement_analysis.reason: Wadgaon (1779) was a rare British military defeat in this period; the Convention of Wadgaon required the British to surrender their gains and was later repudiated by Warren Hastings as unauthorised.

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings accepted the Convention of Wadgaon as a valid agreement and used it as the basis for subsequent negotiations with the Marathas.
statement_analysis.reason: Warren Hastings explicitly repudiated the Convention of Wadgaon as unauthorised, launched coordinated attacks from multiple fronts, and ultimately secured the Treaty of Salbai on better terms — he did not accept Wadgaon as valid.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) included a provision for approximately twenty years of peace between the Marathas and the British East India Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The Salbai Treaty incorporated a 20-year peace clause, which effectively delayed the Second Anglo-Maratha War until 1803 — over two decades later.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct, and a student uncertain about Warren Hastings's response to Wadgaon may accept Statement 2 as plausible.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Wadgaon (1779) as British defeat and Convention is a textbook fact; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Warren Hastings repudiated Wadgaon, did not accept it; claiming he 'accepted' it is factually wrong.
Confirm Statement 3 — Salbai's 20-year peace clause is a standard exam point; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits ambiguity about Warren Hastings's role. Students know Hastings was central to the First Anglo-Maratha War but may not recall the specific detail that he repudiated (rather than accepted) the Convention of Wadgaon. The word 'accepted' is the critical qualifier — Hastings considered Wadgaon an unauthorised agreement and coordinated a multi-front response that superseded it, ultimately achieving Salbai on British terms.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782) demonstrated both Maratha military resilience and the limitations of their confederacy structure.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Battle of Wadgaon (1779) was a rare British setback. The Maratha forces effectively cut off and cornered the Bombay army, forcing the Convention of Wadgaon — a humiliating British withdrawal.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Warren Hastings repudiated the Convention of Wadgaon as an unauthorised agreement made by the Bombay Presidency without his sanction. He launched coordinated military pressure from Bengal and Madras to reverse the outcome, ultimately achieving the Treaty of Salbai.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) contained a 20-year peace provision, effectively postponing the next Anglo-Maratha War until 1803 — an important structural fact for understanding the chronology of Anglo-Maratha conflicts.

Value Addition:
• Salbai's territorial terms: British retained Salsette; Marathas recovered most other wartime Maratha losses.
• The First Anglo-Maratha War demonstrated Maratha resilience but revealed the confederacy's inability to deliver a decisive knockout blow.
• Wadgaon is the only significant British defeat by Maratha forces — frequently tested in competitive exams.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of Maratha-Nizam conflicts — Palkhed, Udgir, Rakshasbhuvan
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Udgir before Rakshasbhuvan, which sounds plausible to students who know both were significant Maratha-Nizam battles and may not have fixed their precise dates.
elimination_logic: Anchor Battle of Palkhed — 1728; this is the earliest and most famous Baji Rao I battle; it must come first.
Place Battle of Rakshasbhuvan — 1763; this was Madhav Rao I's era, after Panipat III.

Correct sequence: Palkhed (1728) → Udgir (1760) → Rakshasbhuvan (1763) → which is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Udgir-Rakshasbhuvan ordering trap works because both battles involved the Nizam and both occurred in the early 1760s. Students who remember 'Udgir and Rakshasbhuvan are both around 1760' but have not fixed the exact years (1760 vs. 1763) will frequently reverse their order. Option (c) exploits this by placing Rakshasbhuvan before Udgir — a tempting error for imprecise learners.
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha-Nizam rivalry produced a series of battles that must be distinguished chronologically.

Correct sequence: Battle of Palkhed (1728) → Battle of Udgir (1760) → Battle of Rakshasbhuvan (1763)

• Battle of Palkhed (1728): First in the series — Baji Rao I's strategic masterpiece; Nizam forced to sign Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon acknowledging Maratha revenue rights in Deccan.
• Battle of Udgir (1760): Second — Maratha victory over the Nizam just before Panipat III; Nizam ceded territories including Bidar area. This is the 'forgotten triumph' of Maratha history because it occurred immediately before the Panipat disaster.
• Battle of Rakshasbhuvan (1763): Third — Maratha victory over the Nizam in Marathwada, occurring after Panipat III during Madhav Rao I's revival phase.

Trap in options: Options (c) and (d) reverse the Udgir-Rakshasbhuvan ordering — the most commonly confused adjacent dates.

Value Addition:
• Udgir (1760) is considered the high point of Maratha military power in the Deccan — immediately before Panipat III reversed the trajectory.
• All three battles were Maratha victories — the Nizam was consistently unable to permanently dislodge Maratha dominance in the Deccan.
• Rakshasbhuvan is often tested in the context of Madhav Rao I's southern revival.

statement_analysis.statement: Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) is credited with administrative development of Pune as a major political and cultural centre and with expansion of Maratha territorial claims into Bengal and Karnataka.
statement_analysis.reason: These achievements specifically belong to Balaji Baji Rao (Peshwa 1740–1761) — Pune's growth as a capital and the Bengal/Karnataka campaigns are hallmarks of his tenure.

statement_analysis.reason: Sawai Madhavrao's reign was conducted under Nana Fadnavis's effective regency — the Peshwa held nominal authority while Nana made actual decisions, closely paralleling the earlier Chhatrapati-Peshwa dynamic.

statement_analysis.statement: Balaji Baji Rao died shortly after receiving news of the Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat, having served as Peshwa until that point.
statement_analysis.reason: Balaji Baji Rao's death (1761) is historically linked to grief following the Panipat disaster; he died shortly after the battle, having been Peshwa throughout the campaign's planning phase.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) identifying Statements 2 and 3 as incorrect is a strong distractor because students who doubt Statement 3's causal claim ('died of grief') may mark it as questionable, creating uncertainty about whether to include it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Pune development and Bengal/Karnataka expansion are correctly attributed to Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb); this is correct, NOT the answer.

Evaluate Statement 2 — Sawai Madhavrao ruled under Nana Fadnavis's regency; claiming he exercised 'direct and effective personal authority without dependence on any ministerial regent' is factually wrong. This IS an incorrect statement.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Balaji Baji Rao did die in 1761 shortly after Panipat; he was Peshwa until that point. This is correct, NOT the answer.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → option (b) — 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the sole incorrect item, but the question's trap is that students uncertain about Statement 3 (the 'died of grief' claim) may mark it as incorrect too, selecting option (c). Statement 3, while including an interpretive element about grief, is factually grounded: Balaji Baji Rao did die in 1761 shortly after Panipat and did serve as Peshwa through that period. The causal claim about grief is a historical tradition, not the falsifiable element — the factual claim (timing of death, tenure) is accurate.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb, Peshwa 1740–1761) from Sawai Madhavrao (Madhavrao II, Peshwa 1774–1795) is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Balaji Baji Rao's tenure saw Pune's development as a major political-administrative centre and the geographic peak of Maratha expansion — into Bengal (1741–1751) and Karnataka (southern campaigns). NOT incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Sawai Madhavrao's reign was under Nana Fadnavis's effective regency. The Peshwa's authority was nominal — a structural repetition of the Chhatrapati-Peshwa dynamic at the Peshwa level itself. The claim of 'direct and effective personal authority without regent dependence' is factually false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Balaji Baji Rao received news of Panipat III in 1761 and died shortly after — historical accounts link his death to the shock of the defeat. He was Peshwa until that moment. NOT incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The period 1740–1761 (Balaji Baji Rao) is the geographic apex; the period 1761–1772 (Madhav Rao I) is the recovery phase.
• Sawai Madhavrao's suicide (1795) triggered the succession crisis that installed Baji Rao II.
• Nana Fadnavis's regency under Sawai Madhavrao is structurally analogous to the Peshwa's dominance under the Chhatrapati.

solution.concept_anchor: Nana Fadnavis — Triple Alliance failure and diplomatic limits
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both that Nana Fadnavis attempted the Triple Alliance AND that it ultimately failed to protect Maratha independence may assume the failure (R) explains the diplomatic achievement (A).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Nana Fadnavis did attempt to forge a Triple Alliance among Marathas, Hyderabad Nizam, and Mysore against British pressure — this is historically documented.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Triple Alliance failed primarily because of mutual suspicion among the three parties, particularly Hyderabad's reluctance and Mysore-Maratha historical rivalry.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. A describes the formation attempt; R describes its failure. The reason Nana attempted the alliance (to counter British pressure) is not explained by the reason the alliance failed (mutual suspicion). R explains the outcome of A, not the cause or nature of A itself.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Nana Fadnavis's diplomatic legacy is defined by his attempt to construct a coalition that could match British power — and by its failure to materialise effectively.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Nana Fadnavis pursued a Triple Alliance (Marathas, Hyderabad Nizam, Tipu Sultan's Mysore) as a diplomatic counter to British expansion — an ambitious multilateral strategy.
• Reason (R): Correct. The alliance collapsed due to mutual suspicion: Hyderabad distrusted both Marathas and Mysore (historical rivals), and Tipu Sultan's aggressive posture made the Nizam wary. British diplomacy also worked actively to prevent the coalition.
• Causal relationship: R describes the reason the alliance failed, not the reason Nana attempted it. A describes the diplomatic initiative; R describes its outcome. These are sequentially related but R is not the causal explanation for A — it is a consequence of A's limitations. A different causal chain (the threat of British expansion) explains why A was attempted.

Value Addition:
• The Triple Alliance failure is sometimes used to illustrate how the Maratha confederacy's structural distrust extended to external allies.
• Tipu Sultan's communications with France (revolutionary) and Nana's diplomacy occurred in roughly the same period — both were anti-British but failed to coordinate.
• After Nana's death (1800), no single Maratha figure could replicate his pan-confederacy diplomatic management.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Bhopal 1738 — Malwa cession qualitative leap over 1719

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Bhopal (1738) represented a qualitatively different achievement from the 1719 Maratha-Mughal agreement because it granted Marathas territorial sovereignty over Malwa rather than merely revenue collection rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1719 treaty gave fiscal rights (Chauth, Sardeshmukhi); the 1738 Treaty of Bhopal gave actual territorial sovereignty over Malwa — a qualitative leap from fiscal extraction to territorial control.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon, concluded after the Battle of Palkhed (1728), granted Marathas territorial control over parts of the Deccan as compensation for their military victory.
statement_analysis.reason: Mungi-Shegaon (1728) granted the Nizam's acknowledgment of Maratha revenue rights (Chauth and Sardeshmukhi) in the Deccan — it did not grant territorial sovereignty; the Marathas did not acquire Nizam's territory through this treaty.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know both treaties involved Nizam may assume the Nizam ceded territory at Mungi-Shegaon (confusing it with the larger Udgir cession of 1760).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — The distinction between 1719 (revenue rights) and 1738 (territorial sovereignty over Malwa) is a standard analytical point in Maratha history; Statement 1 correctly articulates this qualitative difference.

Evaluate Statement 2 — Mungi-Shegaon (1728) was about revenue rights acknowledgment; it did not involve territorial cession. Territorial gains from the Nizam came later at Udgir (1760). Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
Correct answer is (c) — Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is the Mungi-Shegaon/Udgir conflation. Both were agreements with the Nizam involving Maratha gains, but Mungi-Shegaon gave revenue rights while Udgir (1760) gave territorial cessions including Bidar. Students who remember 'Nizam ceded territory to Marathas' without anchoring which agreement produced territorial vs. fiscal concessions will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Two pivotal Maratha agreements must be distinguished: Mungi-Shegaon (1728) for revenue rights, and Bhopal (1738) for territorial sovereignty.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 1719 treaty established fiscal legitimacy (Chauth, Sardeshmukhi rights); the 1738 Treaty of Bhopal established territorial sovereignty over Malwa — the Mughals formally ceded the region. This represents a qualitative shift from being a revenue-extracting power to being a territorial sovereign power.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon (1728, post-Palkhed) required the Nizam to acknowledge Maratha revenue collection rights in the Deccan — a political humiliation for the Nizam, but not a territorial cession. Territorial cessions from the Nizam came much later at Udgir (1760), when he ceded areas including Bidar.

Value Addition:
• The progression — 1719 (revenue rights) → 1728 (Deccan acknowledgment) → 1738 (territorial sovereignty) — charts Maratha power evolution.
• Bhopal (1738) marked the effective end of Mughal control over central India.
• Udgir (1760) was the last major territorial gain before Panipat III — making it the geographic peak of Maratha territorial control.
