solution.concept_anchor: Madhav Rao I — post-Panipat recovery facts

statement_analysis.statement: Madhav Rao I (Peshwa 1761–1772) defeated Hyder Ali of Mysore in military campaigns conducted during his tenure, checking Mysore's northward expansion.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali in 1764 and again in 1767, making Marathas the primary military check on Mysore's expansion before the Anglo-Mysore Wars.

statement_analysis.statement: The internal challenge Madhav Rao I faced from Raghunathrao (Raghoba) was fully resolved through military defeat of Raghoba before Madhav Rao I's death.
statement_analysis.reason: The Raghoba problem was managed and contained during Madhav Rao I's reign but not permanently resolved; Raghoba continued to be a political factor even after Madhav Rao I's death, ultimately causing the succession crisis and Surat Treaty (1775).

statement_analysis.statement: Madhav Rao I died at a young age, and his death is considered a major turning point in Maratha history because it ended the post-Panipat recovery and opened the succession crisis.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhav Rao I died at approximately 27 years of age (1772), and his death removed the only Peshwa capable of sustaining the recovery; the succession crisis that followed directly involved Raghoba and eventually drew in the British.

statement_analysis.statement: Madhav Rao I re-established Maratha tributary authority over Rajput states during his tenure, reversing some of the diplomatic isolation that preceded Panipat III.
statement_analysis.reason: Madhav Rao I's northern campaigns restored Maratha influence over Rajputana, with Rajput states again paying tribute — a reversal of the pre-Panipat alienation of potential allies.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is a strong distractor because Statements 1, 3, and 4 are all correct and well-known; Statement 2's precise qualification (not 'fully resolved') is the subtle trap that converts it to incorrect.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Hyder Ali defeats (1764, 1767) under Madhav Rao I are documented; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Raghoba was 'managed', not 'fully resolved'; he remained active after Madhav Rao's death and caused the Surat Treaty crisis. The word 'fully resolved' makes this incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Madhav Rao I's early death at ~27 and its turning-point significance is a standard fact; correct.
Confirm Statement 4 — Restoration of Rajput tributary relationships is part of the post-Panipat revival narrative; correct.
Three correct (1, 3, 4) → option (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is the qualifier 'fully resolved'. Students who know Raghoba was Madhav Rao I's main internal adversary may recall that Madhav Rao I imprisoned and defeated Raghoba at various points — this is true. But 'fully resolved' is false because Raghoba remained politically active after Madhav Rao I's death and became the central figure in the Surat Treaty crisis (1775). The difference between 'managed' and 'fully resolved' separates precise from approximate knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Madhav Rao I's 11-year reign (1761–1772) is the most underappreciated phase in Maratha history — a genuine recovery from the Panipat catastrophe.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Defeats of Hyder Ali (1764, 1767) made Marathas the first major military check on Mysore's expansion, preceding the British-Mysore confrontation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Raghoba was managed during Madhav Rao I's reign (including periods of imprisonment) but not 'fully resolved'. After Madhav Rao I's death (1772), Raghoba pursued his Peshwaship claim, leading to the Surat Treaty (1775) and the First Anglo-Maratha War.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Death at ~27 years of age (1772) is a documented fact; Madhav Rao I's early death is consistently cited as a critical turning point ending the recovery phase.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Restoration of Rajput tributary relationships was part of Madhav Rao I's northern campaigns, reversing some of the pre-Panipat alliance failures.

Value Addition:
• The Raghoba problem illustrates how internal succession disputes weakened the Marathas as much as external threats.
• Madhav Rao I's campaigns covered Rajputana, Karnataka, and southern India — showing the breadth of his recovery.
• Had Madhav Rao I lived another decade, the trajectory of British expansion in India may have been significantly different — a frequent historical counterfactual.

solution.concept_anchor: Palkhed vs Bhopal — distinct battles, distinct opponents, distinct outcomes
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students know both Palkhed (1728) and Bhopal (1738) involved the Nizam, and may believe the Nizam was the opponent at Bhopal — while the 1738 battle involved a Nizam-supported Mughal force rather than the Nizam acting alone.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Palkhed (1728) was against the Nizam alone; Bhopal (1738) had a different configuration — this option incorrectly maps both to the same opponent.

Eliminate option (c) — While the Nizam was associated with the Bhopal context, the primary framework of Bhopal (1738) was Mughal-Maratha with Nizam backing; describing it as 'Nizam alone' at Bhopal over-simplifies.
Eliminate option (d) — The description of Palkhed as an artillery-based victory is incorrect; Palkhed was a maneuver/supply-line warfare victory.

Confirm option (b) — Palkhed (1728): Baji Rao I vs. Nizam-ul-Mulk alone, won through maneuver warfare, outcome: Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon. Bhopal (1738): Baji Rao I vs. Nizam-backed Mughal forces, outcome: Mughal cession of Malwa through Treaty of Bhopal. This accurately distinguishes both.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (a) and (c) both exploit the 'both battles involved the Nizam' conflation. Students who remember only that both Palkhed and Bhopal featured the Nizam as a party will struggle to distinguish which option correctly maps each battle's specific opponent configuration, tactical character, and treaty outcome. Option (c) is the most dangerous because the Nizam was indeed a factor at Bhopal — but the primary treaty was with the Mughals, not the Nizam alone.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing Palkhed (1728) from Bhopal (1738) is one of the most testable precision requirements in Maratha history.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Both battles did not have identical opponents or outcomes; grouping them as equivalent misrepresents the historical record.
• Option (b): Correct. Palkhed (1728) was Baji Rao I's direct confrontation with Nizam-ul-Mulk, won through cavalry maneuver and supply-line interdiction, producing Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon (Nizam acknowledges Maratha revenue rights). Bhopal (1738) was against a Mughal force supported by the Nizam; Baji Rao I's victory here produced the Treaty of Bhopal — Mughal cession of Malwa to the Marathas.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Bhopal (1738) settlement was primarily with the Mughal authority, resulting in territorial cession of Malwa — framing it as 'Nizam alone' at Bhopal misidentifies the primary party.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Palkhed's fame rests on maneuver warfare — cutting supply lines — not artillery superiority. Artillery as a decisive factor is associated with the Panipat III context (Ibrahim Khan Gardi).

Value Addition:
• Palkhed → Mungi-Shegaon: Revenue rights in Deccan (fiscal gain). Bhopal → Treaty of Bhopal: Malwa cession (territorial gain).
• The two battles together mark the arc of Baji Rao I's strategic achievement.
• Students must anchor: Palkhed = Nizam directly; Bhopal = Mughal cession; both are Baji Rao I's campaigns.

solution.concept_anchor: Confederacy structural flaws — Panipat III failure

statement_analysis.statement: The absence of unified command authority over the diverse Maratha sardars was a structural factor that weakened Maratha military coordination at Panipat III.
statement_analysis.reason: Each sardar maintained independent command authority; the Peshwa's centralised direction was insufficient to override sardar autonomy in the field — a direct expression of the confederacy's structural weakness.

statement_analysis.statement: The Maratha defeat at Panipat III was caused solely by the numerical superiority of Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces over the Maratha army.
statement_analysis.reason: Multiple factors caused the defeat: supply line collapse, alienation of Rajput and Jat allies, political disagreements within the Maratha camp, and superior Afghan cavalry tactics — numerical superiority alone does not explain the defeat, and the 'solely' qualifier makes this incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The Jat chief Suraj Mal's withdrawal from the Maratha camp before Panipat III illustrates the failure of Maratha alliance diplomacy in the period leading up to the battle.
statement_analysis.reason: Suraj Mal withdrew due to disagreements over strategy and Maratha treatment of allied contributions — a concrete example of the Maratha failure to maintain allied cohesion.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Statements 2 and 3 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 2 contains a partial truth (Abdali's forces were indeed formidable), and students may not register the 'solely' qualifier that makes it incorrect.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Lack of unified command is a standard historiographic explanation for Panipat III; correct.

Evaluate Statement 2 — 'Solely' caused by numerical superiority is false; multiple factors including supply collapse, ally alienation, and tactical factors are cited. The word 'solely' makes this incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Suraj Mal's withdrawal as evidence of alliance failure is a documented historical fact; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's 'solely' qualifier is a classic scope-extension trap. Students who recall that Abdali's forces were militarily formidable at Panipat may accept the numerical superiority claim without registering that 'solely' makes it an overstatement. The Maratha defeat was multi-causal — supply line collapse alone is often cited as equally or more decisive than the force disparity.
solution.final_explanation:
Panipat III's causes and consequences require multi-factor analysis — a single-cause explanation invariably fails.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Maratha confederacy's structural weakness — each sardar's autonomy undermining unified command — is a standard explanation for coordination failures during the Panipat campaign.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'solely' is the critical qualifier. Abdali's forces were formidable, but the Maratha defeat resulted from a combination of factors: supply line collapse (Abdali cut off Maratha provisioning), the alienation of Rajput and Jat allies, internal disagreements within the Maratha leadership, and Afghan cavalry tactics. Attributing the defeat solely to numerical superiority is historically reductive.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Suraj Mal (Jat chief of Bharatpur) withdrew from the Maratha camp before the battle — a specific, documented example of Maratha failure to maintain allied commitment through respectful treatment and strategic accommodation.

Value Addition:
• Supply line collapse is often cited by military historians as the single most important material factor in Maratha defeat at Panipat.
• The 'emptying of Maharashtra' refers to the generational loss of Maratha nobility at Panipat — demographic, not just military.
• Post-Panipat: British emerged as ultimate beneficiary; Abdali withdrew without establishing permanent rule.

solution.concept_anchor: Territories where Marathas exercised direct administration vs tribute extraction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) Gujarat is a strong distractor because Gaekwad controlled it and students may associate 'Gaekwad = part Maratha administration' with direct Peshwa administrative control, when Gaekwad exercised semi-autonomous control under the confederacy structure.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: Bengal, Rajputana, and Orissa were areas where Marathas extracted tribute (Chauth) without establishing direct administrative control.

Evaluate Malwa: After the Treaty of Bhopal (1738), Malwa was formally ceded to the Marathas with territorial sovereignty — this is qualitatively different from tribute extraction without direct control.
Bengal, Rajputana, Orissa = tribute extraction; Malwa = territorial sovereignty and direct Maratha administration.
Malwa is the odd one out — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The common-attribute identification trap works because all four territories are associated with Maratha power. The critical distinction is that Malwa came under direct Maratha territorial sovereignty (post-1738 Treaty of Bhopal), while Bengal, Rajputana, and Orissa remained under tribute extraction without direct Maratha administration. Students who associate all four with 'Maratha expansion' without distinguishing administrative versus extractive presence will fail to identify Malwa as the odd one out.
solution.final_explanation:
Maratha engagement with different territories varied fundamentally — some involved direct territorial control, others only tribute extraction.

• Bengal: Maratha Bargi raids (1741–1751) extracted tribute from Bengal Nawabs; Marathas never administered Bengal directly.
• Rajputana: Maratha forces extracted tribute from Rajput states under Baji Rao I and Madhav Rao I; no direct Maratha administration was established.
• Orissa: Ceded to Marathas in 1751 treaty with Alivardi Khan, but operated more as a tributary arrangement managed by Nagpur Bhonsle — limited direct administration.
• Malwa: After the Treaty of Bhopal (1738), Malwa was formally ceded as a territory with Maratha sovereign administration — the Peshwa assigned sardars to govern it directly. This is qualitatively different from tribute extraction.

Malwa is the odd one out — it is the territory where Marathas exercised direct territorial sovereignty, unlike the others where tribute extraction without full administration was the model.

Value Addition:
• The Bhopal (1738) cession of Malwa is the clearest example of Maratha territorial sovereignty expansion.
• Holkar's Indore and Scindia's Gwalior both lay within or adjacent to the Malwa region under direct Maratha confederacy governance.
• The distinction between 'tributary' and 'directly administered' territories is frequently tested in UPSC questions on Maratha governance.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of key Peshwa transitions and constitutional developments
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Balaji Vishwanath's hereditary transformation after Baji Rao I's reign, which appeals to students who think 'greater power = later development' without fixing the specific Peshwa sequence.
elimination_logic: Anchor Event 1: Balaji Vishwanath transforming Peshwaship into hereditary office — 1713–1720; this is the earliest institutional change.
Event 2: Baji Rao I's campaigns — 1720–1740; follows immediately after Balaji Vishwanath.
Event 3: Balaji Baji Rao's peak territorial expansion (Bengal raids) — 1740–1761; next in sequence.
Event 4: Sawai Madhavrao's reign under Nana Fadnavis's regency — 1774–1795; latest of the four. Correct sequence: 1→2→3→4 = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (c) and (d) exploit uncertainty about the precise order of Peshwa transitions. Students who remember individual Peshwas but have not fixed the precise sequence may confuse the constitutional development (hereditary office transformation) with the military expansion phase, or misplace Sawai Madhavrao's regency period relative to Balaji Baji Rao's peak expansion phase.
solution.final_explanation:
The Peshwa period's constitutional and territorial evolution follows a clear sequence.

Correct sequence:
1. Balaji Vishwanath transforms Peshwaship into hereditary office (1713–1720): The foundational institutional change.
2. Baji Rao I's military campaigns establishing Maratha paramountcy (1720–1740): Military expansion phase.
3. Balaji Baji Rao's peak territorial expansion into Bengal and Karnataka (1740–1761): Geographic apex.
4. Sawai Madhavrao's nominal reign under Nana Fadnavis's effective regency (1774–1795): Twilight phase.

This sequence traces the arc from institutional creation → military expansion → territorial peak → structural decline.

Trap: Options (c) and (d) reverse events 1 and 2, or 3 and 4 — exploiting imprecise knowledge of Peshwa succession dates.

Value Addition:
• The sequence 1→2→3 covers the 'rise and peak' narrative; event 4 belongs to the decline phase.
• Madhav Rao I (1761–1772) is not listed here — he fits between events 3 and 4, representing the brief recovery interlude.
• Each Peshwa built on the preceding one's foundation — understanding succession sequence is essential for contextualising individual achievements.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Udgir 1760 — Maratha victory, Nizam cedes territories
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know the Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon resulted from a Maratha-Nizam battle may confuse which battle produced which treaty, assigning Mungi-Shegaon to Udgir.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon followed the Battle of Palkhed (1728), not Udgir (1760); the pairing assigns a 1728 treaty to a 1760 battle.
Eliminate option (b) — Udgir (1760) was a Maratha victory OVER the Nizam, not a Maratha defeat; describing it as a defeat reverses the outcome.

Confirm option (c) — Battle of Udgir (1760) was a decisive Maratha victory over the Nizam; the subsequent settlement required the Nizam to cede territories including the Bidar area and parts of present Osmanabad — a significant territorial gain.
Eliminate option (d) — Rakshasbhuvan (1763) was a separate battle; Udgir (1760) preceded it and had distinct territorial consequences.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) targets the Palkhed-Udgir confusion: both produced Nizam-acknowledging-Maratha-rights agreements, but Mungi-Shegaon follows Palkhed (1728) while Udgir (1760) produced different territorial outcomes. Students who remember 'Maratha victory over Nizam → Mungi-Shegaon' without temporal anchoring will assign the wrong treaty to the wrong battle.
solution.final_explanation:
The Battle of Udgir (1760) deserves attention precisely because it is overshadowed by the Panipat III disaster that followed barely a year later.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon followed the Battle of Palkhed (1728), not Udgir (1760). Assigning Mungi-Shegaon to Udgir confuses two distinct Maratha-Nizam settlements separated by 32 years.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Udgir (1760) was a decisive Maratha victory — the Nizam was defeated, not the Marathas. Describing it as a Maratha defeat reverses the historical outcome.
• Option (c): Correctly matched. The Battle of Udgir (1760) was a decisive Maratha victory; the settlement compelled the Nizam to cede territories including Bidar and surrounding areas — one of the most significant Maratha territorial gains from the Nizam.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Rakshasbhuvan (1763) and Udgir (1760) are separate battles; confusing their territorial outcomes conflates events that occurred three years apart.

Value Addition:
• Udgir (1760) is considered the military apex of Maratha power in the Deccan — followed within months by the Panipat III disaster.
• The Bidar cession gave Marathas control of strategically important Deccan fortifications.
• Students must anchor: Palkhed → Mungi-Shegaon; Udgir → Bidar cession — both Nizam-Maratha but different dates and outcomes.

solution.concept_anchor: Chauth origin under Shivaji — Peshwa expanded scope not origin

statement_analysis.statement: Chauth as an instrument of revenue extraction from non-Maratha territories was introduced by Balaji Vishwanath during the early 18th century as part of his treaty negotiations with the Mughal court.
statement_analysis.reason: Chauth was Shivaji's innovation in the 17th century; Balaji Vishwanath secured formal Mughal recognition of pre-existing Chauth rights in the 1719 treaty but did not introduce the instrument.

statement_analysis.statement: The 1719 Maratha-Mughal agreement gave formal imperial recognition to Maratha claims over Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from the Deccan, but this represented recognition of a pre-existing practice rather than a new grant.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1719 treaty formalised rights that Marathas had been exercising since Shivaji's period; the treaty transformed customary practice into treaty-recognised rights — recognition, not creation.

statement_analysis.statement: Sardeshmukhi was collected by the Marathas as compensation for their role in maintaining order in the Deccan — equivalent in legal basis to the Chauth protection levy.
statement_analysis.reason: Sardeshmukhi was claimed as a hereditary right of the Maratha chief as senior headman (Sardeshmukh) of the Deccan — a distinct legal basis from Chauth (protection levy). They are not equivalent in legal justification.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Statement 3 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 3's error is subtle (equating Sardeshmukhi's legal basis with Chauth's), and students who identify Statement 1 as also incorrect may doubt themselves.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Chauth originated under Shivaji, not Balaji Vishwanath; Balaji Vishwanath secured Mughal recognition of pre-existing rights. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Correctly describes the 1719 treaty as recognition of pre-existing practice, not creation of new rights. This is correct — not the answer.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Sardeshmukhi's legal basis was hereditary headman claim, not protection levy; equating it with Chauth's basis is incorrect. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 reversed the causation: Balaji Vishwanath formalised recognition, but Shivaji originated Chauth. Students who associate 'Balaji Vishwanath + Chauth' because he secured the 1719 treaty may accept Statement 1 as correct without distinguishing 'introduction' from 'recognition'. Statement 3's trap is the conflation of two distinct legal justifications — Chauth (protection) and Sardeshmukhi (hereditary headman claim).
solution.final_explanation:
The Maratha revenue system requires precise attribution: who introduced which instrument, and on what legal basis.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Chauth was introduced by Shivaji as an extraterritorial revenue instrument in the 17th century. Balaji Vishwanath secured formal Mughal recognition of this pre-existing right through the 1719 treaty — a legal formalisation, not an introduction.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 1719 treaty converted customary Maratha Chauth/Sardeshmukhi extraction into treaty-recognised rights — recognition of practice, not creation of new rights. Accurately characterised.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Sardeshmukhi rested on a distinct legal claim — the Maratha chief's hereditary position as Sardeshmukh (senior headman) of the Deccan. Chauth was a protection levy. These are separate legal justifications; treating them as equivalent misrepresents the revenue system.

Value Addition:
• Shivaji claimed Sardeshmukhi on the basis that he was the Sardeshmukh — the paramount headman — of the entire Deccan region.
• The 1719 treaty's significance lay in converting informal extraction into formal treaty right, making Maratha revenue claims legally defensible under Mughal imperial law.
• Chauth was not unique to Marathas — earlier powers also used protection levies; but Shivaji systematised it into a regular administrative instrument.

solution.concept_anchor: Anglo-Maratha agreements and events — precise attribution
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the Treaty of Salbai's outcome description with that of the Convention of Wadgaon, which appeals to students who remember 'Salbai = British retained something' without specifics.
elimination_logic: Confirm A-3: Treaty of Surat (1775) — Raghoba ceded Salsette and Broach to British; this is a locked anchor pair.
Confirm D-4: Convention of Wadgaon (1779) — rare British military reversal requiring British withdrawal; anchor this.

Distinguish B and C: Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War with British retaining Salsette and 20-year peace (B-1); Warren Hastings repudiated Wadgaon but this belongs to the Salbai context — his coordinated multi-front response (C-2) describes his strategic reaction to Wadgaon.
Only option (d) A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 is consistent with all confirmed pairings.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets the Warren Hastings connection. Students know Hastings was central to both repudiating Wadgaon and securing Salbai; they may assign his 'repudiation action' to Salbai rather than correctly placing it as his response to Wadgaon. Option (b) exploits this by shuffling B and C while keeping A and D fixed — forcing students to distinguish Hastings's reaction (to Wadgaon) from the treaty outcome (Salbai).
solution.final_explanation:
The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782) involved multiple agreements that must be carefully distinguished.

Correct pairings:
• A (Treaty of Surat, 1775) — 3 (Raghoba cedes Salsette and Broach to British in exchange for military support): The initiating event that drew British into Maratha succession dispute.
• B (Treaty of Salbai, 1782) — 1 (British retain Salsette, 20-year peace agreed, war ends): The war-ending agreement; British kept Salsette despite the broadly status quo nature of other provisions.
• C (Warren Hastings's strategic response) — 2 (Repudiation of Wadgaon Convention, coordinated multi-front military pressure from Bengal and Madras): Hastings rejected the Bombay army's Wadgaon surrender and reorganised the entire campaign strategy.
• D (Convention of Wadgaon, 1779) — 4 (Humiliating British withdrawal; rare Maratha military success over the Bombay army): The tactical Maratha victory that Hastings then worked to reverse.

Value Addition:
• Wadgaon (1779) is the only significant British battlefield defeat by Maratha forces — frequently tested.
• Salbai's 20-year peace clause delayed the Second Anglo-Maratha War to 1803.
• The First Anglo-Maratha War demonstrated that neither side could deliver a knockout blow — setting up the structural pattern of subsequent Anglo-Maratha conflicts.

solution.concept_anchor: Nature of Maratha presence across different regions — administration vs extraction

statement_analysis.statement: In Bengal, Maratha Bargi cavalry conducted raids (1741–1751) aimed at tribute extraction — Marathas did not establish administrative machinery or territorial governance over Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: The Bengal engagement was explicitly extractive and coercive — no Maratha administrative system was established; the 1751 treaty's Chauth and Orissa provisions were tributary, not administrative.

statement_analysis.statement: In Malwa (post-1738), Marathas exercised direct territorial sovereignty, assigning sardars to govern the region — qualitatively different from their tributary engagement with Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: Treaty of Bhopal (1738) gave Marathas territorial sovereignty over Malwa; sardar assignments (Holkar in particular) constituted direct governance — the opposite of the Bengal model.

statement_analysis.statement: The Nizam's repeated military defeats by the Marathas (Palkhed 1728, Udgir 1760) resulted in the permanent elimination of the Nizam as a political entity in the Deccan.
statement_analysis.reason: Despite repeated defeats, the Nizam survived as a political entity; he continued as a regional power, eventually became a British ally under subsidiary alliance, and the Hyderabad state persisted until 1948 — the Marathas never eliminated the Nizam permanently.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gaekwad's control of Gujarat under the Maratha Confederacy was exercised with significant autonomy, with the Gaekwad maintaining independent diplomatic and administrative operations.
statement_analysis.reason: The Gaekwad was technically subordinate to the Peshwa but operated with considerable autonomy in Gujarat — a manifestation of the confederacy's loose structure where nominal subordination coexisted with practical independence.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is the strongest distractor because Statements 1, 2, and 4 are all correct, and Statement 3's error (permanent elimination of the Nizam) may seem acceptable to students who remember 'Marathas dominated the Nizam repeatedly' without tracking the Nizam's subsequent survival.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Bengal as extractive/tributary without administration is a standard historical characterisation; correct.
Confirm Statement 2 — Malwa post-1738 as directly administered through sardar assignments is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — 'Permanent elimination' is false; the Nizam survived, became a British subsidiary ally, and Hyderabad persisted until 1948. This is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 4 — Gaekwad autonomy in Gujarat within the confederacy framework is correctly characterised; correct.
Three correct (1, 2, 4) → option (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's 'permanent elimination' is a scope-extension trap. Students who recall that the Marathas defeated the Nizam at Palkhed and Udgir may accept that these defeats translated into elimination — they did not. The Nizam's resilience and ultimate survival as a British-protected state is a counter-narrative that requires knowing what happened after the Maratha-Nizam conflicts ended. The word 'permanent' and 'elimination' together make the statement false.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding Maratha expansion requires distinguishing different modes of engagement across regions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Bengal was a tributary/raid zone — Bargi raids extracted Chauth and forced the Nawab to cede Orissa in 1751, but no Maratha administrative presence was established.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Malwa (post-1738) was directly governed through sardar assignments under the confederacy framework — Holkar's Indore being the primary example.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Despite defeats at Palkhed (1728), Bhopal (1738), and Udgir (1760), the Nizam was never eliminated as a political entity. He survived, adapted, signed subsidiary alliances with the British, and the Hyderabad state persisted until India's independence-era integration in 1948.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Gaekwad's Gujarat operations were semi-autonomous — the confederacy structure allowed nominal Peshwa subordination alongside practical independence in local administration and diplomacy.

Value Addition:
• The Nizam's survival despite repeated Maratha defeats reflects the resilience of well-established regional powers even under military pressure.
• Three correct statements (1, 2, 4) yield 'Only three' as the answer.
• The different modes — extractive (Bengal), sovereign (Malwa), tolerant (Nizam), semi-autonomous (Gaekwad) — reflect Maratha pragmatism rather than a uniform imperial policy.

solution.concept_anchor: Maneuver warfare — Palkhed strategy applied to principle
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because the scenario describes a brilliant indirect approach, and students who know Baji Rao I's 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' ideology may associate any Baji Rao I strategy with that concept rather than the specific tactical principle.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — scorched-earth warfare involves destroying resources in one's own or enemy territory; the scenario describes interdicting supply lines without scorching, and the commander is not destroying local resources.
Eliminate option (b) — positional defence involves holding strong defensive positions; the scenario describes offensive mobility, not defensive positioning.
Eliminate option (d) — 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' is an ideological/political concept, not a tactical doctrine; the scenario describes a tactical method, not an imperial ideology.

Confirm option (c) — interdiction of enemy supply lines to force capitulation without pitched battle is precisely the maneuver warfare tactic used at Palkhed (1728); the scenario maps exactly to this principle.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) targets students who associate any description of Baji Rao I's military brilliance with 'Hindu Pad Padshahi'. That concept is a political ideology (Maratha paramountcy), not a tactical doctrine. The scenario describes a specific tactical method — maneuver warfare through supply interdiction — which is the principle exemplified at Palkhed, not an expression of political philosophy. Students who recall 'Baji Rao I = Hindu Pad Padshahi' without distinguishing ideology from tactics will select (d).
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario reconstructs the strategic logic of the Battle of Palkhed (1728) without naming it — testing principle recognition rather than event recall.

Applicable principle: Maneuver warfare through enemy supply line interdiction — achieving military objectives by forcing the adversary into an untenable logistical position rather than engaging in a direct pitched battle.

Mapping to the scenario: The commander avoids direct confrontation, moves behind enemy lines, cuts off provisions and reinforcements, and forces surrender through attrition — exactly what Baji Rao I did against Nizam-ul-Mulk at Palkhed.

• Option (a) — Scorched-earth warfare: Incorrect. Scorched earth involves deliberate destruction of resources (fields, supply depots, towns) to deny them to the enemy. The scenario describes interdiction of supply routes, not destruction of territory.
• Option (b) — Positional defence strategy: Incorrect. The scenario describes an offensive maneuver; positional defence is a passive, hold-ground approach.
• Option (c) — Maneuver warfare through supply line interdiction: Correct. The commander's strategy of encircling, cutting off provisions, and forcing capitulation without a full-scale battle is the defining feature of this tactical approach — and of Palkhed.
• Option (d) — Hindu Pad Padshahi ideology applied to military campaigns: Incorrect. This is a political philosophy articulating Maratha paramountcy — not a tactical doctrine.

Value Addition:
• Palkhed (1728) is studied in military academies as an early example of indirect approach warfare.
• The indirect approach — forcing victory through logistics rather than direct combat — minimises casualties for the attacker.
• The Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon, which followed Palkhed, was the political payoff for this tactical mastery.
